sections.title: Why you do or do not use AI
sections.help: Eleven statements. There are no right answers; we are measuring what drives adoption, not testing you.

questions.text: How much do you agree with each statement?

rows.label: Using AI tools improves the quality of my work
Using AI tools helps me get things done faster

I would rather rely on a person's judgement than an algorithm's
I do not trust AI tools to be accurate about Ethiopian subjects
AI tools do not understand the language or context I work in

questions.note: UTAUT (Venkatesh et al. 2003) extended with algorithmic aversion, following Ayeni et al. (MWAIS 2024), who field the same constructs in Nigeria, Cameroon and Uganda at n=54. Fielding them here at scale with a documented frame makes the Ethiopian result comparable to that work and to any later replication. The three aversion rows are reverse-coded in scoring.

questions.text: How likely are you to use AI tools in your work over the next twelve months?
questions.note: Behavioural intention: the UTAUT dependent variable. Kept separate from B1 (current frequency), so intention and behaviour can diverge, which is where facilitating conditions show up. The top option formerly read “Certain; I already do and will continue”, which a respondent who answered “Never” to B1 could not truthfully pick. Behavioural intention must be answerable by a non-user; that is the whole point of asking it separately from current frequency.

questions.text: What single change would most improve the environment for AI work in Ethiopia?
This one is not a question; it is a check that a person is answering. Please choose “Disagree”.
questions.help: Surveys like this one are sometimes filled in by programs, or by people tapping through without reading. One item that asks for a specific answer tells us how much of that is in the data. It does not affect you either way.
questions.note: Instructed-response attention check. The wording was originally “so we can check for automated responses”, which reads as an accusation to the respondent who IS reading -- the only person who will ever see it properly. It is marked core so it survives the short form: a short questionnaire is more prone to straight-lining, not less.

questions.text: What should Ethiopia's AI policy include that it does not adequately cover today? Choose up to five.
questions.note: Same options as the organisational instrument's I10, so practitioner and institutional views of the same question can be compared directly.

Optional: if Ethiopia does little more on AI over the next five years, what do you think the country looks like in 2031 compared with peers that did invest?
May we contact you about follow-up research or to share results?
How may we reach you? Choose any that suit you.
questions.help: We only ask for what you choose to give, and it is stored separately from your answers.
questions.note: Multi-select rather than one-of: a respondent with an unreliable email and a reliable phone should be able to give both, and follow-up reaches more people if they pick the channel rather than the researcher.

constraints.message: Under 20 with more than ten years of professional experience is unlikely. Please check.
constraints.note: Both items are bands, so only the genuinely impossible corner is worth testing; anything subtler would be a form arguing with a respondent about arithmetic it cannot actually do. Flagged, not blocked -- the answer is recorded either way and the flag is reported as a data-quality statistic.

constraints.message: Strong agreement with both intending to leave and being able to build a career without leaving.
constraints.note: F3.stay1 is reverse-keyed ON PURPOSE. Agreeing strongly with a statement and its opposite is the classic signature of straight-lining, and detecting it is the entire reason a reverse-keyed item is in an attitude scale. Routing it away would delete the detector and leave the scale unable to tell a considered answer from a column of identical taps. Flagged, never blocked, and reported as a data-quality statistic alongside the speeder and planted-item rates.

constraints.message: Has accepted AI work outside Ethiopia, but reports no intention to leave.
constraints.note: Genuinely possible -- remote work for a foreign employer is accepting work abroad without leaving, and F1 has an option for exactly that. Flagged so the analysis can separate the two rather than assume.

constraints.message: Rates their machine-learning ability at the top of the scale, but reports never having built or trained a model.
constraints.note: Self-rated ability against reported practice. The gap is the individual-level twin of the organisational self-versus-computed maturity gap, and is worth measuring for the same reason.
